text: Migo is curious about your evening.

Migo wants to know about your English.
How long have you been learning English?

Migo is curious about food.
Have you ever tried a food you didn’t like?

Yes, I tried durian once and I didn’t like it.

Present perfect with a finished time
Read your sentence again with “{marker}” in mind. Does the verb fit?
“{marker}” is a finished time. Which tense do we use for finished times?
Finished time → past simple. Compare: “She called me last night.” Now try yours.
“{marker}” names a finished time, so we use the past simple. The present perfect connects the past to now, so it doesn’t go with a finished time.

Verb form after have / has
Take another look at the verb after “{aux}”.
After “have” or “has” we use a special form of the verb, and it isn’t always the same as the simple past.
Compare: {exBase} → {exPast} → {exPart}. We say “I have {exPart}”, not “I have {exPast}”. Now try yours.
After “have” or “has” we use the past participle: “have {participle}”, not “have {verb}”.

since without the present perfect
Look at the verb that goes with “since”.
“Since” links a starting point in the past to now. Which tense links the past to now?
Starting point + now → present perfect. Compare: “She has worked here since 2020.” Now try yours.
“Since” gives a starting point, and the situation continues now, so we use the present perfect: “I have lived here since 2018”.

for and since
Check the word in front of your time expression.
We use “for” with how long something lasts, and “since” with when it started.
for + how long (“for three years”). since + when it started (“since 2020”). Now try yours.
Use “for” with a length of time (three years) and “since” with a starting point (2018). Both go with the present perfect.

Same verb, two tenses
Finished time → past simple: “I saw the film yesterday.”
Connected to now → present perfect: “I have seen the film, so I know the ending.”
Finished or still true?
Finished → past simple: “I lived in Rome in 2015.”
Still true now → present perfect: “I have lived in Rome since 2015.”
For or since?
for + how long: “for three years”
since + when it started: “since 2021”
Experience or a finished time?
Experience, no time → present perfect: “I have tried sushi.”
Finished time → past simple: “I tried sushi last year.”
